description: Stored two-factor secrets and backup codes are encrypted with AES-256-CBC and no MAC, so anyone able to write a ciphertext can flip plaintext bits undetected; the IV itself is generated correctly.
The encryption key is decoded as Latin1, keeping only the low byte of each UTF-16 code unit, so a non-ASCII CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY loses entropy and distinct keys can collide on one key value.
CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY both encrypts stored two-factor secrets and app credentials and is the HMAC secret signing OAuth access tokens at OAuthService.ts:448, so one leak yields token forgery.
An unauthenticated GET decrypts a caller-supplied token with unauthenticated CBC whose IV the caller also supplies, then trusts the decoded userId; nothing binds that user to the booking confirmed.
With UNKEY_ROOT_KEY unset the shared limiter returns success for every call after one warning log, so login, signup and slow-mode throttling silently vanish and credential stuffing is unbounded.
The limiter's 5 second timeout fallback returns success, so an attacker who merely slows the rate-limit service, or enough concurrent load, turns every protected endpoint into an unthrottled one.
The limiter's onError handler returns success for any error, so a quota exhaustion, credential rotation or network fault at the rate-limit provider disables throttling across the whole application.
Bot verification returns success whenever its secret is absent or a public end-to-end flag is truthy, and that flag is build-time inlined, so a release built with it set ships the challenge disabled.
The password policy rejects only strings shorter than seven characters, requiring one upper-case letter, one lower-case letter and one digit, so a seven-character credential is permitted.
Sessions are stateless JWTs with no server-side store, so a stolen session cookie stays valid for its full lifetime and neither a password change nor an admin action can revoke it before it expires.
The overridden JWT encoder takes the session lifetime from the user's own editable metadata, so an account holder, or anyone who can write that metadata, extends the validity of an unrevocable token.
Every session-token mint writes the whole token payload, including subject, email and role, to the console-only tslog logger at debug verbosity; no remote transport is wired on this path.
The credentials authorize path logs the whole credentials object, which by its own type declaration at L149 carries email, plaintext password, TOTP code and backup code, at debug verbosity.
The SAML IdP authorize path logs the whole credentials object, whose only field is the single-use SAML authorization code, so that code is written to the log before it has been redeemed.
The jwt callback logs token, user, account and session together on first sign-in, and the account object carries the identity provider's access, refresh and id tokens as clear text.
The OAuth branch of the jwt callback logs the whole account object, whose access_token, refresh_token and id_token fields are the provider credentials themselves, as clear text.
The signIn callback logs the entire params object, which carries the submitted credentials body for the credentials provider and the account tokens plus provider profile for OAuth.

safeStringify JSON.stringifies its argument before tslog sees it, so the maskValuesOfKeys list at logger.ts:7 can never match a nested key and every credential inside a logged object survives as text.
Four hardcoded policies allow script-src 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' https:, so the header offers no barrier at all to injected inline script and any HTML injection becomes script execution.
Every /:path*/embed route ships frame-ancestors * with X-Frame-Options ALLOWALL, so any site may frame a booking page and, with a SameSite=None session cookie, drive authenticated clicks inside it.
With enforcement off the nonce policy builder returns null and the report-only branch is commented out, so the response keeps only the permissive unsafe-inline static CSP from next.config.ts:434.
Over HTTPS the NextAuth session cookie is issued SameSite=None so it accompanies every cross-site request, which removes the browser's built-in defence for authenticated state-changing actions.
Production builds publish browser source maps, handing an attacker unminified client logic, internal module paths and any comment or identifier that hints at server-side structure.
Nonce CSP is enforced only on /auth/login and /login; the other five matcher paths get a nonce but no CSP header, so all remaining routes keep next.config.ts's static unsafe-inline policy.
Dispatch re-fetches the stored subscriber URL with no re-validation; the registration control covers only the tRPC and v2 writers and skips DNS, so a host public at save and private now is fetched.
Only the three tRPC webhook writers and API v2 call this sync validator - v1 calls none - and its own comment says it skips DNS, so a host public at registration and private at delivery defeats it.
The DNS-resolving validator swallows lookup errors and returns valid, so an attacker whose own nameserver deliberately fails the query skips the private-IP check entirely rather than being rejected.
The v1 webhook schema leaves its subscriberUrl check commented out and apps/api/v1 adds no SSRF refinement, so the public create endpoint stores internal targets that tRPC and v2 both reject.
With no secret configured the signature helper returns an empty string and the caller then omits the signature header, so a subscriber cannot tell a genuine delivery from a forged one.
The signature header is added only when the webhook lookup succeeded, and that lookup swallows its own error, so a transient database fault silently sends the payload unsigned instead of failing.
The scheduled row is deleted before its unawaited fetch resolves and the closing allSettled is never awaited, so a delivery that fails or is cut short by process exit is lost with no retry.
The outer catch converts every delivery throw into an ok:false result, so the inner re-throw never runs, allSettled counts the attempt fulfilled and the success tally reports failures as sent.
The payload template only picks a Content-Type; the body is always the JSON envelope, so a non-JSON template makes the request declare form-urlencoded while sending JSON and is ignored.
When a subscriber row carries no secret the signature is the empty string and the X-Cal-Signature-256 header is omitted, so the receiver cannot tell a genuine delivery from a forged one.
The tasker webhook dispatcher fetches the stored subscriber URL with no re-validation and no timeout or abort signal, so a rebound host is reached and a slow sink holds the worker open.
The subscriber's own response text is returned as the result message and logged unbounded on failure, so an attacker-controlled endpoint writes arbitrary content of any length into the log stream.
A webhook operationId is generated and logged but never placed on the task payload or the outbound request, so deliveries carry no X-Request-Id, traceparent or operation id to correlate against.
The builder stage defaults NEXTAUTH_SECRET to the literal secret and promotes it to ENV, so a build passing no --build-arg compiles the web app with a known key held in that stage's metadata.
The builder stage defaults CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY to the literal secret and promotes it to ENV, so a no-argument build holds a known encryption and token-signing key in that stage's metadata.
No stage in the web image declares a USER, so the application starts as root and any code-execution defect in it inherits full container privileges instead of an unprivileged account's.
The API image declares no USER either, so the NestJS process starts as root and a compromise of it can modify the container's writable layer and reach whatever its capabilities permit.
The tracked environment template assigns CRON_API_KEY a live-looking 32 character lowercase hexadecimal token; it is the exact secret ten cron endpoints compare against. Value deliberately withheld.
A third-party action is referenced by mutable branch in a job holding contents write and a GitHub App token, so whoever can push that branch gains write access to this repository.
Installs performed through this composite action disable immutable installs, so a resolution absent from yarn.lock is accepted silently in every workflow that calls it, weakening lockfile integrity.
A production runtime dependency of the API is declared as latest, so any lockfile refresh adopts whatever upstream published since, with no manifest diff for a reviewer to notice or approve.
The one suppressed advisory is justified in writing, yet it silences the Yarn auditor that is the only dependency gate here while the pinned XML parser carries five further unaddressed advisories.
Across the integration authority set 37 direct external imports are undeclared in their owning workspace, so 17 packages including express, qs and next-auth resolve only by hoisting.
The Google OAuth2Client is imported directly from googleapis-common at 13 sites while no workspace manifest declares it, so it resolves by hoisting from transitive 5.1.0 or 7.0.1 copies.
Seventeen cron and workflow handlers authenticate a shared secret with plain !== or Array.includes and none uses a timing-safe API; fifteen also accept that secret in the ?apiKey= query string.
The SMS scheduler gates on a non-constant-time secret compare, so a timing-recovered secret only triggers reminders already queued in the two-hour window early or twice; it cannot author new ones.
The sync secret is compared with a non-constant-time !== only after a system-wide-admin API-key gate returns 403 and a deployment gate returns 501, so a timing-recovered secret is useless on its own.
The Helpscout webhook JSON-parses and Zod-validates the body before verifying its HMAC, and compares the digest with a non-constant-time !==; only database access follows verification.
The cron secret is taken from the ?apiKey= query string as well as the Authorization header, so it lands in access, proxy and referrer logs; fifteen handlers read it that way, eleven under api/cron.
The Google Calendar webhook compares x-goog-channel-token only when GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_TOKEN is set, so with that variable absent the check is skipped and any anonymous caller drives calendar sync.
The Retell webhook JSON.parses the raw body before the missing-signature 401 at L230 and Retell.verify at L241, so an unauthenticated malformed payload faults the handler instead of being rejected.
The BTCPay webhook looks up the payment by caller-supplied invoiceId before the HMAC check at L85, and its 404, 200 and 400 replies differ, giving an anonymous caller a payment-state oracle.
The Feishu webhook logs the entire request body at L53 and again at L60 inside the matched branch, so the verification token and app_ticket are written as clear text; neither key is masked.
The Feishu handler repeats the Lark defect: the message-receive and chat-create branches perform no token check before invoking the bot sender, so unauthenticated input reaches provider POSTs.
The Lark webhook logs the entire request body at L53 and again at L60 inside the matched branch, so the verification token and app_ticket are written as clear text; neither key is masked.
The im.message.receive_v1 and p2p_chat_create branches run before any verification-token check and call the bot sender unawaited, so an unauthenticated POST drives authenticated Lark API calls.
The shared recurring-event count is a bare z.number() with no int, min or max, so every bound is delegated to consumers and only the v1 create path documents one, relative to the event type.
The recurrence interval is an unbounded number, so zero, negative and fractional values reach recurrence expansion instead of being rejected at the schema boundary where the contract is declared.
Booking guest lists are unbounded string arrays, so a single request can enqueue arbitrarily many invitation emails and make the platform's own mail reputation the delivery vehicle for the abuse.
The paid-booking price is an unbounded number, so negative and fractional amounts pass schema validation and any correctness of the charge depends entirely on checks further down the payment path.
The public booking body accepts a bare recurringCount with no bounds, so the amplification limit for a recurring booking is whatever the handler happens to enforce rather than a declared contract.

Event-type duration is unbounded on the duplicate path while the sibling create path constrains it to a positive integer, so the same field has two different contracts and the weaker one is reachable.
The embed iframe accepts messages from any origin; its only authenticity test is the payload field originator equal to CAL, which the sender chooses, so any framing page satisfies it trivially.
Having passed only a payload-field check, the listener invokes whichever member of its parent interface the message names and forwards that message's argument, giving unverified-origin dispatch.
The parent-side embed SDK listens for messages without checking event.origin then fires the action manager the message names, so any frame or opener can raise arbitrary embed events on the host.
The embed preview surface calls the Cal SDK method named in an unverified message with that message's argument, so a hostile window handle turns the preview into arbitrary SDK invocation.
Every command the SDK sends into the booking iframe uses targetOrigin *, so prefill values and configuration are readable by whatever origin occupies that frame; the code's own comment flags it.
The iframe broadcasts every embed event, booking-success payloads included, with targetOrigin *, so whichever site frames the booker receives attendee data it was never authorised to see.
All CAL: analytics and booking events are posted to window.opener with targetOrigin *, so any page that opened the booking tab receives the full event payload regardless of its origin.
The reroute dialog's listener filters on a message type only and never on event.origin, so a hostile opener can forge a reschedule-success message and steer the operator to a booking of its choosing.
HitPay's hook acts on any window message with no origin check, so a framing page can forge loaded/toggle/success/error; its wildcard send exposes checkout data only if the nested iframe goes hostile.
tRPC has no default per-user limiter: authedProcedure adds none and the per-user one is commented out, so coverage is endpoint-specific - 13 handlers in 6 families opt in, bookings and slots none.
The payment handler serialises the caught error into its 404 body, and a missing payment makes schemaPaymentPublic.parse throw, so ZodError issue paths and expected types reach the caller.

Payment authorisation is applied after an unscoped fetch and the outcomes differ, 401 for a real payment owned by someone else against 404 for one that does not exist, giving a cross-tenant id oracle.
The v1 booking read includes the whole related user row, materialising twoFactorSecret and backupCodes that the projected response never returns, against the select-over-include rule in AGENTS.md.
The shared v1 chain supplies authentication and throttling but no resource authorisation, so ownership is left to route families - 82 method modules behind 42 dispatchers - in two divergent styles.
Thirty non-test suppression comments across apps/ and packages/ name a linter this repository no longer runs, with four more in tests and one in scripts/; nine non-test comments waive Prisma include.
The allow-list compiles * to .* which also matches / ? and #, so a pattern meant to permit a subdomain admits any host merely carrying the expected text in its query, and a bare * admits all.
Authenticated POST /v2/oauth/:clientId/authorize behind NextAuthGuard validates body.redirectUri with the permissive matcher, then appends the authorization code to it, so a crafted URI captures it.
Platform access-token requests are origin-checked with the same permissive matcher and only when an Origin header is present, so omitting it skips matching; browsers must also pass ALLOWED_ORIGINS.
The proxy mounts v1 at the root before v2 and connect dispatches in order, so /v2/* is expected to be answered by v1 and never reach v2's guard chain. Requires runtime confirmation to claim exploit.

Both proxy targets are declared with no path filter, rewrite, origin change or forwarded-header option, so unauthenticated callers with no cf-connecting-ip header share the proxy's own IP rate bucket.
The validation pipe returns target and value in every error and the HTTP exception filter then logs that exception with the full request body and headers, so rejected payloads reach caller and logs.
Winston ships application logs to Axiom only when AXIOM_TOKEN and AXIOM_DATASET are both set; the console transport is unconditional, so egress past the trust boundary is deployment-dependent.
Tag regexes are built per component key at L219 and per entry of a fixed 11-tag list at L319; the lazy dotall <tag>(.*?)</tag> form measures quadratic in unterminated opening tags.
The HTTP exception filter logs the full request body plus the Authorization and X-Cal-Client-Id headers filterReqHeaders retains, so a rejected OAuth token call still records its client secret.
Every HttpException reply embeds exception.getResponse() as error.details, so the validation pipe's target-and-value error objects are returned verbatim to the caller on any malformed request.
The shared header filter used by every logging site re-emits Authorization verbatim instead of dropping it, so bearer tokens and Basic client credentials are written in full at each call.
The global response interceptor logs every response body verbatim plus the caller's email, so the OAuth token endpoint writes the access and refresh tokens it just issued into the log stream.
Global request middleware logs every request body verbatim with the Authorization header, so POST /v2/auth/oauth2/token writes client secrets, auth codes and PKCE verifiers to the log stream.
PlatformOAuthClient.redirectUris is required in schema.prisma:2156 but the migration creates a nullable TEXT[] and the live column is nullable, so the origin allow-list can be called on a null array.
